summary: DHCPv6 prefix delegation lets a router hand a block of IPv6 addresses to another router. This RFC adds an option that lets the delegating side exclude one specific sub-prefix from the block it hands out, for example one already in use on the link between the two routers. It updates RFC 3633.

eli5.summary: A big pizza is handed to your friend, but you say keep one slice for me. The option tells the receiver which one piece of the delegated address block is not theirs to use.

questions: how to exclude a prefix in dhcpv6 prefix delegation
what is dhcpv6 option pd exclude
how does dhcpv6 prefix delegation exclude a prefix
subtitle: Lets a DHCPv6 server carve one prefix out of a delegated block, such as the one already used on the link.

tldr.problem: RFC 3633 says a prefix delegated to a requesting router cannot be used by the delegating router, so the delegating router needs two non-aggregatable routes to one customer.
tldr.mechanism: A new DHCPv6 option, OPTION_PD_EXCLUDE (67), sits inside OPTION_IAPREFIX and names exactly one prefix within the delegated prefix that the requesting router must not assign downstream.
tldr.outcome: The link prefix can come out of the same delegated block, so one aggregated route can represent a customer. The option is optional and updates RFC 3633.

today: RFC 6603 is a Proposed Standard from May 2012 and updates RFC 3633. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6603 defines an optional mechanism and a related DHCPv6 option for excluding one specific prefix from a delegated prefix set during DHCPv6-based prefix delegation. It updates RFC 3633.

It targets deployments where a single aggregated route or prefix has to represent one customer, rather than one prefix for the link between the delegating and requesting routers and another for the customer network. It is intended for networks where each requesting router is on its own layer-2 domain.
sections.eli5: Normally a router that gives away a block of addresses cannot use any of them itself. This note says it can keep one piece back for itself.

sections.title: The Problem With Plain Delegation
sections.content:
Section 12.1 of RFC 3633 limits DHCPv6 prefix delegation: a prefix delegated to a requesting router cannot be used by the delegating router. The delegating router therefore ends up with two non-aggregatable routes toward a customer, one for the link to the requesting router and one for the customer site behind it.

Some architectures make this awkward. A host, for example a mobile router that is also a requesting router, may always have a single /64 prefix on its uplink, with the delegating router as its first-hop router. That /64 may need to be aggregatable with the delegated prefixes, for example a /56. The difficulty is combining prefix delegation with stateless (RFC 4862) or stateful (RFC 3315) address autoconfiguration when the advertised /64 is also part of the delegated prefix.
sections.eli5: It is like a landlord who gives you a whole floor but also needs the hallway on it. Without a way to say so, the landlord needs a separate address for the hallway and the floor.

sections.title: The Exclude Option Idea
sections.content:
The new option, OPTION_PD_EXCLUDE (option code 67), excludes exactly one prefix from a delegated prefix. It is carried in the IAprefix-options field of OPTION_IAPREFIX, and there can be at most one such option in each OPTION_IAPREFIX.

With it, a requesting router can be delegated a prefix such as a /56, while the delegating router uses one prefix such as a /64 from that same set on the link where they exchange DHCPv6 messages. The delegating router puts the excluded prefix in the option, and the requesting router MUST NOT assign it to any of its downstream interfaces.

To signal support, a requesting router includes the option code in an OPTION_ORO option in a Solicit, Request, Renew or Rebind message. A delegating router may include the code in an OPTION_ORO in a Reconfigure message to indicate that the requesting router should request the option.
sections.eli5: The router that gives out the block writes a note saying which piece is off limits. The router that receives the block promises not to hand that piece out to anyone behind it.

sections.title: The Prefix Exclude Option Format
sections.content:
The option has four parts: the option code (OPTION_PD_EXCLUDE, 67), option-len, prefix-len and a variable-length IPv6 subnet ID of 1 to 16 octets. The option-len is 1 plus the subnet ID length in octets, so a valid value is between 2 and 17.

prefix-len is the length of the excluded prefix in bits. It MUST be between the delegated prefix's OPTION_IAPREFIX prefix-length plus 1 and 128.

The subnet ID holds the bits of the excluded prefix that come after the delegated prefix length, that is, prefix-len minus the OPTION_IAPREFIX prefix-length bits, starting at the bit position equal to that prefix-length. These bits MUST be left-shifted to start at a full octet boundary (a shift of the prefix-length mod 8 bits) and MUST be zero-padded to the next full octet boundary. The RFC gives C-like pseudocode for this encoding.

The excluded prefix MUST be part of the delegated prefix, and it shares the preferred-lifetime and valid-lifetime of the encapsulating OPTION_IAPREFIX. The option MUST only appear in the IAprefix-options field, and any prefix excluded from the delegated prefix MUST be carried in OPTION_PD_EXCLUDE options within that OPTION_IAPREFIX.

The worked example excludes 2001:db8:dead:beef::/64 from the delegated prefix 2001:db8:dead:bee0::/59. The option-len is 2, the prefix-len is 64, and the subnet ID octet carries the bits 01111000, which is 0xef shifted left by 59 mod 8 = 3 bits, with 3 zero-padded bits.
sections.eli5: The note says how long the reserved piece is and then spells out only the part of its address that differs from the big block, squeezed into whole bytes.

sections.title: How Routers Use the Option
sections.content:
The requesting router finds a delegating router as in Section 11 of RFC 3633. If it implements this specification it SHOULD include the option code in the OPTION_ORO of its Solicit messages. When Advertise messages arrive, it uses the prefixes received in OPTION_PD_EXCLUDE, in addition to the advertised prefixes, to choose a delegating router. If an Advertise has no such option, the requesting router MUST fall back to normal behavior from Section 11.1 of RFC 3633.

On the delegating side, an OPTION_ORO with the option code tells the server that the client supports this feature. If the Solicit also holds an IA_PD option, the delegating router can delegate a prefix that includes the prefix already assigned to the requesting router's uplink, and it puts that prefix in OPTION_PD_EXCLUDE in the Advertise. If the code is absent, the delegating router MUST fall back to normal behavior (Section 11.2 of RFC 3633). A server that does not support the feature acts as specified in RFC 3633.

The requesting-router-initiated exchanges work the same way, using a Request instead of a Solicit. To return prefixes in a Release message, the requesting router MUST include the delegated prefixes in the IA_PDs along with the excluded prefix, and MUST NOT use the option to introduce a new excluded prefix for which it did not originally get a valid binding. If a Release contains such a new excluded prefix, the delegating router MUST reply with the Status Code NoBinding for that IA_PD option.

The requesting router must also create sink routes for the delegated prefixes minus the excluded prefixes, for example a sink route for each delegated prefix plus more specific routes for the excluded ones.
sections.eli5: The receiving router says it understands the trick, and the giving router then marks the reserved piece. If either side does not know the trick, they just do things the old way.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The RFC says the option adds no new security considerations beyond those in RFC 3633. DHCPv6 security is covered in Section 23 of RFC 3315, and RFC 3633 gives recommendations for protection against prefix delegation attacks.

For IANA, the DHCPv6 option code OPTION_PD_EXCLUDE (67) was reserved from the DHCPv6 option codes registry.
sections.eli5: Adding the reserved piece does not open any new doors for troublemakers. The same safety advice as before still applies.

fields.name: option-len
fields.desc: 1 plus the subnet ID length in octets; valid values are 2 to 17.

fields.name: prefix-len
fields.desc: Length of the excluded prefix in bits.
